title: ABO Groups, Bombay Phenotype, Cross-Matching, Components, TRALI, and TACO

steps.tx: The ABO blood group system is governed by the ABO gene on chromosome 9q34, which encodes specific glycosyltransferase enzymes that add terminal monosaccharide sugars to a pre-existing H antigen polysaccharide core. The A allele encodes **alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase enzyme activity**, attaching N-acetylgalactosamine to form the A antigen. The B allele encodes alpha-galactosyltransferase, adding D-galactose to generate the B antigen. The O allele carries a single base-pair deletion causing a frameshift that produces an enzymatically inactive protein, leaving the unmodified H antigen intact on erythrocyte membranes.
steps.say: The ABO blood groups are determined by glycosyltransferase enzymes that attach terminal sugar molecules to a precursor carbohydrate core called the H antigen. The A allele encodes an enzyme that adds N-acetylgalactosamine, creating the A antigen. The B allele encodes an enzyme that adds D-galactose, creating the B antigen. The O allele carries a frameshift mutation producing an inactive enzyme, leaving the H antigen unmodified on red blood cells.

steps.tx: The rare **Bombay blood phenotype**, designated Oh, results from homozygous inheritance of the recessive h allele (hh genotype) on chromosome 19. Patients lack functional alpha-1,2-fucosyltransferase 1 (FUT1), the enzyme required to attach L-fucose to precursor oligosaccharide chains to synthesize the H antigen core. Lacking H substance, Bombay individuals cannot synthesize A or B antigens regardless of their ABO genotype. In their serum, Bombay individuals produce potent, complement-fixing IgM and IgG antibodies against A, B, and H antigens, and can receive red cells safely only from another Bombay individual.
steps.say: The Bombay blood phenotype is an extraordinarily rare condition caused by homozygous recessive inheritance of the h allele. Affected individuals cannot synthesize the H antigen core because they lack the fucosyltransferase enzyme that attaches L-fucose. Because they have no H antigen, they cannot form A or B antigens either. Bombay individuals produce strong, complement-fixing antibodies against A, B, and H antigens, so they can safely receive transfusions only from another Bombay donor.

left.title: Standard Group O Phenotype
points: Genotype: OO with functional H gene (H/H or H/h)
Carries abundant H antigen on red cell membranes
Serum contains anti-A and anti-B, but NO anti-H
Can receive blood from any standard Group O donor

right.title: Bombay (Oh) Phenotype
points: Lacks H antigen entirely on red cell membranes
Serum contains potent anti-A, anti-B, AND anti-H
Must receive blood strictly from a Bombay Oh donor

steps.tx: The Rhesus blood group system is encoded by two closely linked homologous genes, RHD and RHCE, on chromosome 1p36. The **RhD surface antigen** is the most potent protein immunogen in transfusion medicine. Unlike naturally occurring ABO antibodies, Rh antibodies are immune-mediated IgG molecules formed only following exposure through transfusion or feto-maternal haemorrhage. When an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus, maternal IgG anti-D antibodies can cross the placenta during subsequent pregnancies, causing severe immune-mediated fetal haemolysis, hydrops fetalis, and erythroblastosis fetalis, prevented by administering anti-D immunoglobulin.
steps.say: The Rh system is clinically second only to the ABO system. The D antigen is the most immunogenic protein antigen on red cells. Rh-negative individuals do not have naturally occurring antibodies; they produce IgG anti-D antibodies only after being exposed to Rh-positive blood during a transfusion or pregnancy. If an Rh-negative mother becomes sensitized, her anti-D antibodies cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies to cause fetal haemolytic disease, preventable by routine Rh-immune globulin prophylaxis.

steps.tx: An **acute haemolytic transfusion reaction** is a catastrophic, life-threatening emergency caused by transfusing ABO-incompatible red blood cells, almost invariably resulting from clerical or patient-identification errors. Pre-existing recipient IgM isohaemagglutinins bind foreign transfused erythrocyte antigens, triggering immediate, massive complement activation through the classical pathway. Intravascular haemolysis releases free haemoglobin, provoking severe flank pain, burning at the infusion site, high fever, hypotension, and shock. The release of red cell stroma and inflammatory cytokines triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation and acute renal failure from haemoglobinuric nephropathy.
steps.say: An acute haemolytic transfusion reaction is an ABO disaster that occurs when incompatible red cells are accidentally transfused into a patient, almost always due to clerical error. Recipient IgM antibodies immediately bind foreign red cells and fix complement, triggering explosive intravascular haemolysis. Patients develop sudden fever, chills, flank pain, and shock. Free haemoglobin and cell stroma flood the kidneys and bloodstream, plunging the patient into acute renal failure and DIC.

vis.caption: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction, the ABO catastrophe cross-matching exists to prevent.

steps.tx: Pre-transfusion compatibility testing is a rigorous multi-tier procedure designed to prevent haemolytic transfusion reactions. The protocol incorporates forward blood grouping (testing patient red cells with reagent anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D antisera) and reverse grouping (testing patient serum against reagent A1 and B red cells) to confirm ABO concordance. An antibody screen detects unexpected non-ABO red cell antibodies using the **indirect antiglobulin test**. Finally, a cross-match incubates recipient serum with donor erythrocytes, verifying that no preformed antibody causes agglutination or complement-mediated lysis.
steps.say: Pre-transfusion testing prevents fatal transfusion errors through three distinct safety steps. First, ABO and Rh typing perform forward grouping to detect red cell antigens and reverse grouping to detect serum antibodies. Second, an antibody screen using the indirect antiglobulin test checks patient serum for unexpected non-ABO antibodies like Kell or Duffy. Finally, a major cross-match mixes recipient serum directly with donor red cells to ensure complete in vitro compatibility before the unit is released.

rows: Reagent A1 and B red blood cells

steps.tx: Stand in front of the component shelf and read each label in turn. One bag holds concentrated red cells, the next plasma rich in clotting factors, another the cold insoluble cryoprecipitate fraction, and the last a platelet concentrate kept at room temperature. Choosing the right **blood component** for the deficit in front of you is the daily discipline of modern transfusion practice.
steps.say: On this shelf, packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate and platelet concentrate sit as separate labelled bags. Modern transfusion means choosing the blood component that matches the actual deficit.

steps.tx: Transfusion-related acute lung injury is the leading cause of transfusion-associated mortality, defined as new acute respiratory distress syndrome developing within six hours of transfusion without pre-existing circulatory overload. Pathogenesis involves an **immune neutrophil-mediated capillary leak**: donor plasma contains high-titer anti-human leukocyte antigen (anti-HLA) or anti-human neutrophil antigen (anti-HNA) antibodies, typically from multiparous female donors. These antibodies bind recipient neutrophils sequestered within pulmonary capillaries, triggering elastase release, massive endothelial damage, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.
steps.say: Transfusion-related acute lung injury, or TRALI, is the leading cause of transfusion fatalities. Within six hours of transfusion, patients develop acute hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. TRALI occurs when anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies in donor plasma, usually from multiparous female donors, bind and activate recipient neutrophils sequestered in pulmonary capillaries. Neutrophils release toxic proteases, causing alveolar capillary leak and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema with completely normal cardiac pressures.

left.title: TRALI (Capillary Leak)
points: Does NOT respond to diuretic therapy; requires ventilation

right.title: TACO (Volume Overload)
points: Hydrostatic volume overload from rapid infusion
Responds dramatically to intravenous furosemide diuresis

steps.tx: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload is a frequent, preventable hydrostatic pulmonary complication occurring during or within twelve hours following rapid or excessive blood component transfusion. Unlike TRALI, the primary pathophysiological defect is acute volume expansion in patients with compromised cardiopulmonary reserve, elderly individuals, or chronic renal disease. Clinical presentation features acute respiratory distress, severe hypertension, tachypnoea, jugular venous distension, S3 gallop, and bilateral basilar crackles. Serum **brain natriuretic peptide elevation** confirms myocardial stretch, and prompt administration of intravenous furosemide with upright positioning rapidly resolves symptoms.
steps.say: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload, or TACO, is hydrostatic pulmonary edema caused by infusing too much volume too quickly into patients with borderline cardiac or renal function. Within hours of transfusion, patients experience acute dyspnea, marked hypertension, engorged neck veins, and bilateral pulmonary crackles. Unlike TRALI, serum BNP is markedly elevated due to acute ventricular stretch, and giving intravenous furosemide diuresis produces prompt clinical improvement.

steps.tx: Modern blood banking separates whole blood donations into specific therapeutic components to maximize resource utilization and minimize volume hazards. Transfusion of **packed red blood cells** is indicated for acute symptomatic anaemia, with one unit predictably elevating adult haemoglobin by one gram per deciliter and haematocrit by three percent. Platelet concentrates treat severe thrombocytopenia, fresh frozen plasma restores all clotting factors in dilutional coagulopathy or liver failure, and cryoprecipitate provides concentrated fibrinogen, factor VIII, and von Willebrand factor for hypofibrinogenemia.
steps.say: Whole blood is routinely fractionated into specific components to treat precise clinical deficits. One unit of packed red blood cells raises adult haemoglobin by one gram per deciliter. Platelet transfusions replenish platelets in consumptive or hypoplastic marrow failure. Fresh frozen plasma replaces all coagulation factors in severe liver failure, while cryoprecipitate provides concentrated fibrinogen and factor eight to treat hypofibrinogenemia and massive obstetric haemorrhage.

rows: Increases Hb by 1 g/dL per unit
All soluble clotting factors and albumin
Increases factor levels by 2% to 3% per unit
Fibrinogen (>150 mg), Factor VIII, vWF, FXIII
Elevates fibrinogen by 50 to 100 mg/dL per pool

quiz.q: What immunodominant terminal sugar is attached to the H antigen core to form the blood group A antigen?
quiz.explain: The A allele encodes an alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase that attaches N-acetylgalactosamine to the H antigen core to produce the A antigen.

quiz.q: What genetic and phenotypic defect defines the Bombay blood phenotype (Oh)?
options: Homozygous recessive hh genotype lacking the FUT1 enzyme needed to synthesize the H antigen
Deletion of the ABO locus on chromosome 9 resulting in complete lack of plasma isohaemagglutinins
Inability to synthesize RhD protein due to deletion of the RHD gene
Failure to express CD55 and CD59 on the erythrocyte membrane
quiz.explain: The Bombay phenotype is caused by homozygous recessive hh mutations in the FUT1 gene on chromosome 19, preventing synthesis of the H antigen core.

quiz.q: What clinical and hemodynamic feature distinguishes transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) from transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)?
options: Normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and lack of response to diuretics in TRALI
Markedly elevated serum brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) in TRALI
Development of severe hypertension and jugular venous distension in TRALI
Rapid clinical resolution upon administering intravenous furosemide in TRALI
quiz.explain: TRALI is a non-cardiogenic capillary leak with normal wedge pressure that does not respond to diuretics, whereas TACO is hydrostatic volume overload with elevated BNP responding to diuretics.
